nameStory: Onychonema filiforme doesn't have a widely-used common name, but its scientific name tells an interesting story. 'Onychonema' comes from Greek words meaning 'claw thread,' referring to the distinctive claw-like projections on these microscopic algae, while 'filiforme' means 'thread-like' in Latin. If we had to give it a common name, 'Thread Claw Alga' would capture its essence perfectly!
description: This is a microscopic freshwater green alga that you'll need a magnifying glass or microscope to truly appreciate. Each individual cell is incredibly tiny - much smaller than the period at the end of this sentence - and shaped like a delicate cylinder with distinctive claw-like projections. The cells often link together to form short, thread-like chains that drift freely in the water. Though invisible to the naked eye individually, colonies can sometimes create a faint greenish tinge in very clean pond water.

idTips.label: Claw-like projections
idTips.description: Under magnification, you'll see distinctive curved, claw-shaped extensions protruding from the cell walls - these look like tiny grappling hooks

idTips.label: Cylindrical cells
idTips.description: Each cell is shaped like a tiny tube or cylinder, much longer than it is wide, with smooth, glassy-looking walls

idTips.label: Chain formation
idTips.description: Cells often connect end-to-end to form short, delicate chains that look like microscopic green beads on a string

idTips.label: Bright green color
idTips.description: The cells have a fresh, vibrant green color - like the bright green of new spring leaves

idTips.label: Free-floating habit
idTips.description: Unlike many algae, these don't attach to rocks or plants but drift freely through the water column

habitat: Look for this rare alga in pristine, nutrient-poor ponds and lakes with very clean, soft water - the kind of crystal-clear mountain tarns or kettle ponds you might find in New Hampshire's White Mountains or Vermont's Green Mountains. It's extremely sensitive to pollution and typically occurs in acidic to neutral waters with low mineral content. You're most likely to find it in remote, undisturbed water bodies surrounded by coniferous or mixed forests.

seasonality.spring: Peak season for observation as waters warm and microscopic life becomes active. Look for faint greenish tinges in clear pond water during late spring.
seasonality.summer: Continues to be present but may be harder to spot as other algae become more abundant. Best observed during cooler morning hours.
seasonality.fall: Still active but populations may begin to decline as temperatures drop. September can be excellent for observation in warm, sunny weather.
seasonality.winter: Largely dormant under ice cover, though some cells may persist in deeper waters that don't freeze completely.

funFact: This microscopic alga is so incredibly rare that it's been documented only once in all of New England - making anyone who spots it again a genuine scientific contributor! Its claw-like projections aren't just for show - they may help it grab onto tiny particles or other algae as it drifts through the water, like a microscopic grappling hook system.
confusionNotes: Under low magnification, it might be confused with other thread-like green algae like Spirogyra, but those lack the distinctive claw projections and have spiral-shaped chloroplasts inside. Remember: if you see the 'claws,' you've found something very special!
contextualKnowledge: This species represents one of nature's most overlooked treasures - the incredible diversity of microscopic life in our freshwater ecosystems. Most people walk past thousands of these tiny organisms without ever knowing they exist, yet they form the foundation of aquatic food webs and are indicators of water quality.
compareHints: Since this is the only Onychonema species documented in New England, compare it with other desmid algae in the same family. Unlike the half-moon shaped Closterium or the intricate star-shaped Micrasterias, Onychonema has a simple cylindrical form. The key difference is always those distinctive claw-like projections - no other desmid in our region has quite the same feature.
